claim: Twenty-four subjects participated in Experiment 1 with MEG recordings.
source: Twenty-four subjects participated in Experiment 1 and their brain activities were recorded using a 306-channel magnetoencephalography (MEG) system (Elekta Neuromag system, Helsinki, Finland).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing the experimental methods.

claim: Memory behavioral performance exhibited the typical recency effect (2nd item > 1st item) in Experiment 1.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the memory behavioral performance exhibited the typical recency effect, that is 2nd > 1st item (N = 24, 1st item: mean = 0.77, s.e. = 0.012; 2nd item: mean = 0.79, s.e = 0.013; paired t-test, df = 23, t = 2.18, p = 0.039, Cohen's d = 0.45), consistent with previous findings (e.g. Broadbent and Broadbent, 1981; Burgess and Hitch, 1999; Gorgoraptis et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2018; Jones and Oberauer, 2013).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and referenced to Figure 1B, with citations to previous literature.

claim: The 2nd item showed steeper psychometric function slope than the 1st item in Experiment 1.
source: When plotting the psychometric function of the proportion of clockwise response as a function of angular difference between the probe and the cued WM grating, the 2nd item showed steeper slope than the 1st item (Figure 1C; 1st item: mean = 0.11, s.e. = 0.009; 2nd item: mean = 0.14, s.e = 0.015; paired t-test, df = 23, t = 2.64, p = 0.015, Cohen's d = 0.54).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of psychometric function slopes with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Orientation information can be successfully decoded from MEG signals in a time-resolved manner during the encoding period.
source: Therefore, orientation information could be successfully decoded from MEG signals in a time-resolved manner.
evidence: Supported by IEM decoding analysis results showing significant orientation representations during encoding.

claim: The 1st orientation showed information representation right after the 1st grating presentation.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, the 1st orientation (blue) showed information representation right after the 1st grating (0.05–0.39 s, corrected cluster p = 0.002; 0.5–0.88 s, corrected cluster p < 0.001; 1.13–1.4 s, corrected cluster p = 0.002), and neural representation of the 2nd orientation (red) emerged after the 2nd grating (1.06–1.5 s, corrected cluster p < 0.001; 1.57–1.86 s, corrected cluster p = 0.008).
evidence: Supported by time-resolved decoding analysis with statistical significance testing, referenced to Figure 2C.

claim: The decoding performance for both orientations gradually decayed to baseline around 0.5 s after the offset of the 2nd item, suggesting the WM network entered activity-silent states.
source: Moreover, the decoding performance for both the 1st and 2nd orientations gradually decayed to baseline, around 0.5 s after the offset of the 2nd item, suggesting that the WM network now entered the activity-silent WM states (Rose et al., 2016; Stokes, 2015; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on observed decoding patterns and cited literature on activity-silent working memory states.

claim: The 2nd orientation showed earlier activation (0.26 to 0.43 s) than the 1st orientation (0.67 to 0.76 s) after the PING stimulus during retention.
source: Interestingly, instead of being activated simultaneously, the 1st and 2nd orientations showed distinct temporal profiles, that is the 2nd orientation showed earlier activation (T2: from 0.26 to 0.43 s, corrected cluster p = 0.011) than the 1st orientation (T1: from 0.67 to 0.76 s, corrected cluster p = 0.030), with approximately 0.3 s temporal lag in-between.
evidence: Supported by time-resolved decoding analysis after PING stimulus with statistical significance testing.

claim: There is approximately 0.3 s temporal lag between the 2nd and 1st item reactivations after PING stimulus.
source: Interestingly, instead of being activated simultaneously, the 1st and 2nd orientations showed distinct temporal profiles, that is the 2nd orientation showed earlier activation (T2: from 0.26 to 0.43 s, corrected cluster p = 0.011) than the 1st orientation (T1: from 0.67 to 0.76 s, corrected cluster p = 0.030), with approximately 0.3 s temporal lag in-between.
evidence: Calculated from the temporal difference between significant reactivation windows.

claim: The 1st and 2nd items are stored in different latent states of the WM network.
source: The results suggest that the 1st and 2nd items, instead of residing in equally excitable states, tend to be stored in different latent states of the WM network.
evidence: Inferred from the distinct temporal reactivation profiles observed after PING stimulus.

claim: The recency effect covaried positively with the 2nd item reactivation.
source: Specifically, the recency effect covaried positively with the 2nd item (Figure 3E, right panel; Pearson's correlation, N = 24, r = 0.50, p = 0.013) and negatively with the 1st item (Figure 3E, left panel; Pearson's correlation, N = 24, r = −0.55, p = 0.005).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between neural reactivation and behavioral recency effect, referenced to Figure 3E.

claim: The recency effect covaried negatively with the 1st item reactivation.
source: Specifically, the recency effect covaried positively with the 2nd item (Figure 3E, right panel; Pearson's correlation, N = 24, r = 0.50, p = 0.013) and negatively with the 1st item (Figure 3E, left panel; Pearson's correlation, N = 24, r = −0.55, p = 0.005).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between neural reactivation and behavioral recency effect, referenced to Figure 3E.

claim: The 2nd – 1st reactivation difference was correlated with the recency effect.
source: As shown in Figure 3F, consistently, the 2nd – 1st reactivation difference was correlated with the recency effect (Pearson's correlation, N = 24, r = 0.47, p = 0.02).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between reactivation difference and behavioral recency effect, referenced to Figure 3F.

claim: Twenty-four new subjects participated in Experiment 2.
source: Twenty-four new subjects participated in Experiment 2.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing Experiment 2 methods.

claim: In Experiment 2, the 1st and 2nd items showed similar memory performance with no significant recency effect.
source: Interestingly, the 1st and 2nd items showed similar memory performance (Figure 4B; 1st item: mean = 0.77, s.e. = 0.011; 2nd item: mean = 0.78, s.e = 0.011; paired t-test, df = 23, t = 1.57, p = 0.13, Cohen's d = 0.32), and the psychometric functions did not differ in slopes for the 2nd and 1st orientations (Figure 4CD; N = 24, 1st item: mean = 0.11, s.e. = 0.008; 2nd item: mean = 0.12, s.e = 0.009; paired t-test, df = 23, t = 1.38, p = 0.18, Cohen's d = 0.28).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 2, referenced to Figure 4B and 4CD.

claim: Recency effect tends to be weakened when the ordinal structure is not needed to be retained in WM.
source: Thus, recency effect tends to be weakened when the ordinal structure is not needed to be retained in WM.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of behavioral results between Experiment 1 and Experiment 2.

claim: The reactivation profiles during the delay period in Experiment 2 did not show the backward pattern as observed in Experiment 1.
source: In contrast, the reactivation profiles (marginally significant trend) during the delay period in Experiment 2 (Figure 4G; 0.1–0.2 s; 1st item, p = 0.056, one-tailed; 2nd item, p = 0.019, one-tailed) did not show the backward pattern as observed in Experiment 1 (see the reconstructed channel response in Figure 2—figure supplement 1EF).
evidence: Supported by comparison of decoding results between experiments, referenced to Figure 4G and supplementary figures.

claim: The difference course between the 1st and 2nd decoding performances in Experiment 2 did not reach statistical significance.
source: Consistently, the difference course between the 1st and 2nd decoding performances did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4H); corrected cluster p > 0.5.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of decoding differences in Experiment 2, referenced to Figure 4H.

claim: The sum of the 1st and 2nd decoding performance in Experiment 2 showed significant responses.
source: Interestingly, different from Experiment 1 (Figure 3C), the sum of the 1st and 2nd decoding performance showed significant responses (Figure 4I; 0.1–0.2 s, corrected cluster p = 0.024), somewhat supporting their common reactivation profiles.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of summed decoding performance in Experiment 2, referenced to Figure 4I.

claim: The 2nd – 1st reactivation difference showed marginally significant difference between Experiment 1 and 2.
source: Finally, as shown in Figure 4J, the 2nd – 1st reactivation difference (i.e., backward reactivation index) showed marginally significant difference between Experiment 1 and 2, within two temporal windows (0.35–0.42 s, independent t-test, cluster p = 0.058; 0.59–0.67 s, independent t-test, cluster p = 0.043).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison between experiments, referenced to Figure 4J.

claim: Experiment 2 did not show the reactivation-recency correlations compared to Experiment 1.
source: Furthermore, Experiment 2 did not show the reactivation-recency correlations either (Figure 4K), compared to Experiment 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in Experiment 2, referenced to Figure 4K and supplementary figures.

claim: Twenty-four new subjects participated in Experiment 3 (behavioral experiment).
source: Given the inherent time lag between the two sequentially presented items, the passive memory decay is seemingly a very straightforward interpretation for the recency effect. To further characterize the recency effect in terms of passive memory decay and sequence structure, we performed a behavioral experiment on 24 new subjects.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript text describing Experiment 3 methods.

claim: Experiment 3 showed significant main effects in both serial position (recency effect) and memory decay.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, significant main effects in both serial position (i.e. recency effect; F(1,23) = 7.03, p = 0.014, η2 = 0.23) and memory decay (F(2,23) = 5.21, p = 0.009, η2 = 0.19) were observed in the behavioral experiment, and there was no interaction effect (F(2,23) = 2.04, p = 0.14, η2 = 0.08).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 3, referenced to Figure 5A.

claim: There was no interaction effect between serial position and memory decay in Experiment 3.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, significant main effects in both serial position (i.e. recency effect; F(1,23) = 7.03, p = 0.014, η2 = 0.23) and memory decay (F(2,23) = 5.21, p = 0.009, η2 = 0.19) were observed in the behavioral experiment, and there was no interaction effect (F(2,23) = 2.04, p = 0.14, η2 = 0.08).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of behavioral data in Experiment 3, referenced to Figure 5A.

claim: Memory performance of items in a list is determined by both passive memory decay and their positions in the sequence.
source: The results thus confirm that memory performance of items in a list would be determined by both passive memory decay and their positions in the sequence (e.g. 1st or 2nd).
evidence: Inferred from the main effects observed in Experiment 3.

claim: Sequence structure context shapes the way WM items are stored in the human brain and essentially influences memory behavior.
source: Taken together, sequence structure context shapes the way WM items are stored in the human brain and essentially influences memory behavior.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experimental and modeling results.

claim: A PING stimulus can transiently perturb the WM network to reactivate stored information and its associated latent states.
source: Critically, during the maintaining period, a high-luminance PING stimulus that does not contain any orientation information was presented, aiming to transiently perturb the WM network so that the stored information and its associated latent states could be assessed.
evidence: Based on the experimental design and cited literature on impulse-response approaches.

claim: An impulse-response approach efficiently reactivates WM representations by presenting a PING stimulus.
source: An impulse-response approach, by presenting a PING stimulus to transiently perturb the WM system, efficiently reactivates WM representations (Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on cited literature describing the impulse-response method.

claim: Attended but not unattended items are successfully reactivated by PING stimulus.
source: Moreover, attended but not unattended item is successfully reactivated, implying that top-down attention modulates the latent states WM items reside in Wolff et al., 2017; Wolff et al., 2020.
evidence: Based on cited literature on attention modulation of WM reactivation.

claim: Information can be stored in synaptic weights of the network without sustained activities (activity-silent view).
source: Interestingly, recent modeling and empirical studies propose that, in addition to maintenance via sustained or serial reactivations (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2003; Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Vogel and Machizawa, 2004), information could also be stored in synaptic weights of the network, that is activity-silent view (Miller et al., 2018; Mongillo et al., 2008; Rose et al., 2016; Sprague et al., 2016; Stokes, 2015; Trübutschek et al., 2017; Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on cited literature on activity-silent working memory mechanisms.

claim: Serial position effect shows that recently presented items have better memory performance compared to early ones.
source: A typical example is the serial position effect for sequence memory, that is the recently presented item shows better memory performance compared to early one (Broadbent and Broadbent, 1981; Burgess and Hitch, 1999; Gorgoraptis et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2018; Jones and Oberauer, 2013).
evidence: Based on cited literature on serial position effects in memory.

claim: A sequence of items elicits serial and temporally compressed reactivations, reflecting a memory consolidation process.
source: Previous neural recordings demonstrate that a sequence of items would elicit serial and temporally compressed reactivations, which might reflect a memory consolidation process that reorganizes the incoming inputs (Bahramisharif et al., 2018; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Huang et al., 2018; Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019; Siegel et al., 2009; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996).
evidence: Based on cited literature on neural reactivations during memory consolidation.

claim: Structure context largely influences memory behavior.
source: Structure context largely influences memory behavior, but how it is implemented in the brain remains unknown.
evidence: Stated as motivation for the study, based on general knowledge of memory research.

claim: Neural representations of WM items could not be generalized from the encoding to maintaining periods.
source: Finally, the neural representation of WM items could neither be generalized from the encoding to maintaining periods, nor across items in the reactivations triggered by PING stimulus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), further advocating that WM items embedded in the sequence structure context are reorganized in varied latent states.
evidence: Supported by cross-temporal generalization analysis, referenced to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neural representations of WM items could not be generalized across items during retention.
source: Finally, the neural representation of WM items could neither be generalized from the encoding to maintaining periods, nor across items in the reactivations triggered by PING stimulus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), further advocating that WM items embedded in the sequence structure context are reorganized in varied latent states.
evidence: Supported by cross-item generalization analysis, referenced to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: WM items embedded in sequence structure context are reorganized in varied latent states.
source: Finally, the neural representation of WM items could neither be generalized from the encoding to maintaining periods, nor across items in the reactivations triggered by PING stimulus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), further advocating that WM items embedded in the sequence structure context are reorganized in varied latent states.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of generalization across time and items in decoding analysis.

claim: Memory information is represented in alpha-band activities during the activity-silent period.
source: Meanwhile, even during the presumably 'activity-silent' period, memory information is still represented in the alpha-band activities (Bocincova and Johnson, 2019; Fahrenfort et al., 2017; Sutterer et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on cited literature on alpha-band representations during working memory.

claim: Alpha-band activities show sustained reactivation profiles for both 1st and 2nd orientations prior to and after the PING stimulus.
source: Our control analysis based on alpha-band activities during retention supports the view and reveals sustained reactivation profiles (prior to and after the PING stimulus) for both 1st and 2nd orientations (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by control analysis of alpha-band decoding, referenced to Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Active sustained representation and STP-based activity-silent storage operate together to mediate working memory.
source: Therefore, two types of mechanism – active, sustained representation and STP-based 'activity-silent' storage –operate together to mediate the working memory process, and future studies could examine their possible distinct functions.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of broadband and alpha-band analyses.

claim: Top-down attention modulates latent states that WM items reside in.
source: Top-down attention modulates latent states that WM items reside in. For instance, the immediately task-relevant item is in a more excitable state and tends to be first reactivated, compared to ones that are potentially task-relevant in the future (e.g. Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012; Rose et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on cited literature on attention modulation of working memory states.

claim: WM items in the present study are equally task-relevant and have the same probability to be tested during recalling.
source: Notably, WM items in the present study are equally task-relevant and have the same probability to be tested during recalling, and the results thus could not be explained in terms of attentional modulation.
evidence: Based on the experimental design where both items have equal probability of being tested.

claim: The results cannot be explained in terms of attentional modulation.
source: Notably, WM items in the present study are equally task-relevant and have the same probability to be tested during recalling, and the results thus could not be explained in terms of attentional modulation.
evidence: Inferred from the equal task relevance of items in the experimental design.

claim: Multiple items located in different excitable states according to their bottom-up saliency levels would be reactivated at different phases within an alpha-band cycle.
source: A theoretical model posits that multiple items, located in different excitable states according to their bottom-up saliency levels, would be reactivated at different phases within an alpha-band cycle (Jensen et al., 2012; Jensen et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited theoretical models of working memory organization.

claim: Reversed replay has been observed during break after spatial experience.
source: In fact, reversed replay has been observed in many circumstances, for example during break after spatial experience (Foster and Wilson, 2006), performing a reasoning task (Kurth-Nelson et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on cited literature on reversed replay phenomena.

claim: During structure learning, a forward replay in spontaneous activities reverses in direction when paired with reward.
source: A recent study shows that during structure learning, a forward replay in spontaneous activities would reverse in direction when paired with reward (Liu et al., 2019), implying the involvement of reinforcement learning principles (Schultz et al., 1997; Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: Based on cited literature on replay direction and reinforcement learning.

claim: The item located in the late position of a list might serve as an anchoring point in memory for other items.
source: Thus, a possible interpretation for the backward reactivation is that the item located in the late position of a list might serve as an anchoring point in memory for other items and is in turn maintained in a more excitable latent state, since the recent item receives less inference and is more reliable for memory retrieval.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the backward reactivation findings.

claim: The recent item receives less interference and is more reliable for memory retrieval.
source: Thus, a possible interpretation for the backward reactivation is that the item located in the late position of a list might serve as an anchoring point in memory for other items and is in turn maintained in a more excitable latent state, since the recent item receives less inference and is more reliable for memory retrieval.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about why recent items might be in more excitable states.

claim: Experiment 2 has been carefully matched with Experiment 1 in many characteristics including same stimuli, WM task, and task difficulty.
source: Experiment 2 served as a control experiment to test a straightforward alternative explanation (passive memory decay) and has been carefully matched with Experiment 1 in many characteristics, for example same stimuli, WM task, task difficulty.
evidence: Description of experimental design considerations.

claim: Subjects in Experiment 2 retained two orientations rather than their relative angle in WM.
source: Second, the behavioral results of Experiment2 are largely accounted for by the angular difference between the to-be-recalled orientation and probe but not by that between the two orientations, confirming that subjects retained two orientations rather than their relative angle in WM.
evidence: Supported by generalized linear mixed-effects model analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Orientation information for both items is precisely represented in terms of the task-relevant dimension (big/small labels) in Experiment 2.
source: First, orientation information for both items is indeed precisely represented in terms of the task-relevant dimension (big/small labels) in Experiment 2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis based on big/small labels, referenced to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The computational model incorporates passive memory decay and sequence structure to understand recency behavior.
source: We built a computational model (Bays et al., 2009) that incorporates passive memory decay and sequence structure aiming to understand the recency behavior.
evidence: Description of the computational modeling approach with citation.

claim: The model fitting separates the memory decay influence and confirms that sequence context mostly accounts for the recency effect.
source: The model fitting separates the memory decay influence and confirms that it is the sequence context that mostly accounts for the recency effect.
evidence: Summary of computational modeling results.

claim: Group-level Bayesian model selection revealed that the protected exceedance probability for the model with different σ and same β was higher (0.65) than the other two models (both 0.17).
source: The group-level Bayesian model selection revealed that the protected exceedance probability for the first model was higher (0.65) than the other two (both 0.17).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian model comparison analysis.

claim: MEG recordings together with computational model convergingly advocate an essential role of sequence context in WM and its neural implementation.
source: Taken together, MEG recordings together with the computational model convergingly advocate an essential role of sequence context in WM and its neural implementation, that is reorganizing WM items into different latent states of the neural network.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating MEG and modeling results.

claim: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision with no history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
source: All subjects had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, with no history of psychiatric or neurological disorders.
evidence: Description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: All experiments were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: All experiments were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: Statement of ethical compliance.

claim: All participants provided written informed consent prior to the start of the experiment, which was approved by the Research Ethics Committee at Peking University.
source: All participants provided written informed consent prior to the start of the experiment, which was approved by the Research Ethics Committee at Peking University (2019-02-05).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval and informed consent.

claim: Participants completed 280 trials in total in Experiment 1.
source: Participants should complete 280 trials in total (determined in a pilot EEG study that used the same number of trials and found successful decoding).
evidence: Description of experimental design with justification from pilot study.

claim: Each subject completed five blocks with each containing 56 trials in Experiment 1.
source: Specifically, each subject completed five blocks with each of which containing 56 trials.
evidence: Description of experimental structure.

claim: Participants completed 864 trials in total in Experiment 3, in three blocks.
source: Participants completed 864 trials in total, in three blocks.
evidence: Description of experimental design for Experiment 3.

claim: MEG data were recorded at 1000 Hz sampling frequency.
source: MEG data were recorded at 1000 Hz sampling frequency.
evidence: Description of MEG recording parameters.

claim: The data was offline band-pass filtered between 2 and 30 Hz.
source: Specifically, the data was offline band-pass filtered between 2 and 30 Hz.
evidence: Description of MEG preprocessing steps.

claim: All data was downsampled to 100 Hz.
source: All data was then downsampled to 100 Hz.
evidence: Description of MEG preprocessing steps.

claim: The minimum number of trials per orientation for decoding analysis was set to be 37 in each subject, resulting in at least 259 trials per subject.
source: Next, to ensure that each orientation had the same number of trials, we set the minimum number of trials per orientation for decoding analysis to be 37 in each subject, which resulted in at least 259 trials per subject.
evidence: Description of data selection criteria for decoding analysis.

claim: Only posterior MEG channels (52 planar gradiometers, 26 magnetometers for parietal sensors; 48 planar gradiometers, 24 magnetometers for occipital sensors) were used for analysis.
source: Since here we focused on the orientation representations in the MEG response, only posterior MEG channels, including parietal sensors (52 planar gradiometers, 26 magnetometers) and occipital sensors (48 planar gradiometers, 24 magnetometers), were used for further analysis.
evidence: Description of channel selection for analysis.

claim: An inverted encoding model (IEM) was used to reconstruct orientation information from MEG signals.
source: To assess the time-resolved orientation information from the MEG signals, we used an inverted encoding model to reconstruct the orientation of the grating stimulus from the neural activities at each time point.
evidence: Description of the decoding method used.

claim: The IEM method has been previously used on features such as color, orientation, and spatial location.
source: This method has been previously used on many features, such as color (Brouwer and Heeger, 2009), orientation (Brouwer and Heeger, 2011; Ester et al., 2015; Kok et al., 2017; Myers et al., 2015), and spatial location (Sprague et al., 2014; Sprague et al., 2016; Sutterer et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on cited literature on IEM applications.

claim: The response in each sensor can be approximated as a linear sum of underlying neural populations encoding different values of the feature-of-interest.
source: One assumption of the model is that the response in each sensor could be approximated as a linear sum of underlying neural populations encoding different values of the feature-of-interest (e.g. orientation) separately, and therefore, by grouping the contributions from many sensors, we could achieve an estimation of the underlying neural population responses.
evidence: Description of the theoretical basis of the IEM method.

claim: The slope time courses were smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (s.d. = 40 ms).
source: The slope time courses were further smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (s.d. = 40 ms, Wolff et al., 2017).
evidence: Description of data smoothing procedure with citation.

claim: A cluster-based permutation test with 1000 permutations was performed for statistical testing.
source: A cluster-based permutation test (FieldTrip, cluster-based permutation test, 1000 permutations) (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007) was then performed.
evidence: Description of statistical testing method with citation.
